subject: Two jump dispersals from one node?

messages.author: 77157785e2f788ce
messages.subject: Two jump dispersals from one node?
parts:
Dear Nick, 

I am working on a biogeographical analysis using the DEC+J model and find some equivocal reconstructions. Specifically, there is a lineage with ancestral area (A) that splits in two clades that each are unique to a particular area (B and C). The equivocal scenarios are either A->B->C or A->C->B. This makes sense as it is impossible to estimate which of the two is better. 

However, I can imagine a third scenario that is missing from the results: namely that the lineage dispersed from A to B AND C (i.e. jump dispersals to two different areas, see image below). 

Because this scenario is never reconstructed, I suspect that this is a limitation of the analysis (indeed, there is no such scenario in the BioGeoBEARS supermodel graphic). 

My question is why such a scenario is not reconstructed and if there is a workaround? 

Thanks! 

Robin van Velzen

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Two jump dispersals from one node?
parts:
Hi Robin!  Thanks for the question!

It is true that scenario is not programmed in the standard models,
therefore it will not be reconstructed (but see below*).

It wouldn't be that hard to add the scenario as an option, but the
biological justification seems weak. I totally believe that an ancestral
population could produce jump dispersals to two regions basically
simultaneously ("basically simultaneously", i.e. close together as measured
over millions of years).  However -- why would that simultaneously make the
ancestor go extinct?

Even if one figured out a reason for that, these models (DEC etc)
effectively assume zero lineage extinction, i.e. a Yule or pure-birth
process, i.e. the observed tree is treated as the complete tree.  Adding
lineage extinction requires an BiSSE-like model or something similarly
elaborate (and computationally very slow for large numbers of states --
BiSSE has only 2 states).  This assumption sucks, but it is very common in
many phylogenetic comparative methods (or it is effectively assumed, if
extinction is estimated but comes out near zero, which is common).

Hope this helps!
Cheers, Nick

PS: If you *did* see such a scenario in an ancestral-states plot under the
standard models, it would be a case of this:

The plot of most-probable states is not the same thing as the best joint
history
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_joint

...and related to my usual mantra...

Ancestral range estimation, not ancestral area reconstruction
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#ace_not_arr

PPS: And, when interpreting biogeographical ancestral ranges plots,
remember that neither traditional parsimony nor traditional continuous-time
likelihood models are good interpretive frameworks for the likelihood
models in biogeography:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#intro

Cheers!
Nick

messages.author: 77157785e2f788ce
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Two jump dispersals from one node?
parts:
Hi Nick, 

Many thanks for the quick response and explanations. This confirms what we suspected. 

I was referring to the stochastic mappings but we did not see such a scenario in the ancestral states plot either - just the two equivocal scenarios. But I think a two-jump dispersal is at least theoretically plausible in our case (if one can assume one 'jump' dispersal with immediate extinction in the ancestral area, why not two dispersals with extinction immediate after the second dispersal). But I totally see how this would be difficult to model realistically without taking into account lineage extinction (or lack of sampling). 

I will write something short along those lines in our discussion. 

Thanks again & cheers!

Robin

parts: Hi, leaving for Evolution 2017 in a bit, brief comment:

On Mon, Jun 19, 2017 at 5:28 PM, Robin van Velzen <robinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Nick, 

Many thanks for the quick response and explanations. This confirms what we suspected.

But I think a two-jump dispersal is at least theoretically plausible in our case (if one can assume one 'jump' dispersal with immediate extinction in the ancestral area,

A one-jump dispersal event definitely does not assume immediate extinction in the ancestral area!  The ancestral population continues, and is represented by the other lineage at the lineage-splitting event.  I suppose you could call this "pseudo-extinction" of the "ancestral species" when one species splits into two, but clearly that's not real extinction.

E.g. ancestor lineage lives in B;

Figure 1:

BBBBBBBBBB

Jump dispersal happens, founds a new population in A:

Figure 2:

BBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
                             A
 
...both continue:


Figure 3:

BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
                             AAAAAAAAAAAAAA

We show this in typical phylogenies like this, basically because it is annoying/difficult to re-do the tree drawing software (and would be especially difficult when probabilities are not 100% etc.):


Figure 4:

                            BBBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
BBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
                             AAAAAAAAAAAAAA


But, Figure 4 and Figure 3 are showing you identical events.

Cheers!
Nick
